examples.label: FTP client commands
examples.command:
ls
ls -R
status
get Important\ Notes.txt
put testupload.txt
exit

examples.label: Find FTP NSE scripts
examples.command:
sudo nmap --script-updatedb
find / -type f -name ftp* 2>/dev/null | grep scripts

notes: Always try anonymous login first (anonymous:anonymous). Note the banner/software+version for known CVEs. `ls -la` for hidden files; download everything with `wget -m`. Writable root often means webshell upload if FTP serves a web dir.

recommended.note: Brute the login if anonymous fails.
Use the server to scan other hosts.

name: FTP - Enumeration
description: Enumerate FTP: try anonymous login, browse/mirror files, run NSE scripts, and interact manually with nc/telnet/openssl to read the banner and test commands.

defense.why_it_works: FTP is a clear-text protocol, meaning credentials and data can be sniffed if an attacker is on the network. Anonymous FTP login is a misconfiguration common on internal servers whose administrators assume they are not discoverable — 'configuration errors are found on servers that the administrators think are not discoverable.' This attitude means internal systems are often left without hardening.
defense.prerequisites: Network access to an FTP service (TCP 21), ideally permitting anonymous/guest login.
defense.impact: A directory listing and downloadable files (possibly credentials or sensitive data) plus the server version for CVE matching.
defense.detection: [MITRE T1046 AN1583] Monitor for execution of network enumeration utilities (nmap, netcat, net.exe, ping.exe, tracert.exe) in short succession, particularly when chained with lateral movement tools or system enumeration commands. [AN1584] Sequential ping, arp, or traceroute commands issued from bash scripts or interactive shells to map remote hosts are a strong behavioral indicator.
defense.artifacts: An FTP connection and login command in the server log; plaintext control-channel traffic visible to sniffers.
defense.prevention:
Disable anonymous FTP access. Enable TLS/SSL (FTPS) to encrypt credentials and data in transit. Set hide_ids=YES to prevent local usernames from appearing in directory listings, removing targets for brute-force. Deploy fail2ban to block IPs after repeated failed login attempts — described in the module as 'a standard implementation of any infrastructure.'

[MITRE T1046 M1042] Disable or remove unnecessary services and functionality that expose attack surface. [M1030] Implement network segmentation to limit the set of hosts reachable from any given compromised system. Use firewalls to restrict which source addresses can reach each service port.
defense.misconfiguration: The FTP server allows anonymous login (username 'anonymous', any password), which may expose sensitive files. Additionally, FTP transmits credentials in cleartext over the network — any passive eavesdropper on the same network segment can capture usernames and passwords. FTPS or SFTP should replace FTP in all cases.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# vsftpd — anonymous login enabled (common default):
# /etc/vsftpd.conf:
anonymous_enable=YES       # allows login as 'anonymous'
anon_upload_enable=YES     # anonymous can upload files
anon_mkdir_write_enable=YES # anonymous can create directories
write_enable=YES
# No encryption — credentials and data in cleartext (port 21)
defense.secure_config:
# vsftpd — disable anonymous, enforce encryption:
# /etc/vsftpd.conf:
anonymous_enable=NO        # disable anonymous login
local_enable=YES
write_enable=NO            # read-only by default
chroot_local_user=YES      # jail users to their home directory

# Enable FTPS (TLS):
ssl_enable=YES
rsa_cert_file=/etc/ssl/certs/vsftpd.crt
rsa_private_key_file=/etc/ssl/private/vsftpd.key
force_local_logins_ssl=YES  # require TLS for all logins
force_local_data_ssl=YES    # require TLS for all data transfers
ssl_tlsv1_2=YES

# Better alternative: use SFTP (SSH subsystem) instead of FTP entirely:
# sshd_config: Subsystem sftp /usr/lib/openssh/sftp-server
# chroot via Match User block
